# The Missing `<!DOCTYPE>` and PHP Logic Error in Your Form Submission

You have a working form structure, but when you click submit, the browser displays the raw source code of `myform.php` instead of rendering the processed data. This is a classic symptom of two distinct issues: one is an HTML syntax omission preventing proper MIME type negotiation, and the other is a logical flaw in how your PHP script outputs its result.

### The Browser's Protocol Mismatch

The primary reason you see raw code is that the browser does not recognize `myform.php` as executable server-side code. Modern browsers expect a specific declaration at the very start of every HTML file: the `<!DOCTYPE html>` tag. Without this, the browser assumes the document is written in older HTML 4.01 Transitional standards. In that legacy mode, the browser does not perform automatic MIME type detection. It treats the response as plain text rather than HTML, which triggers a security warning or simply renders the source code directly to the user.

Adding `<!DOCTYPE html>` before the `<html>` tag forces the browser into Standards Mode. This ensures it correctly interprets the Content-Type header sent by PHP (`text/html`). Once the browser recognizes the content as valid HTML, it will stop displaying the raw tags and render the output you intend.

### The Logic Error in `myform.php`

Even after fixing the DOCTYPE, your current implementation of `myform.php` will likely break if the form is submitted without data or if there are any unexpected characters. Your PHP code attempts to access `$_POST["name"]` directly:

```php
<?php
$name = $_POST["name"];
// ... other variables
?>
<body>
<?php echo $name; ?>
</body>
```

This approach is fragile. If a user submits the form without filling out a field, or if the input contains special characters like quotes or angle brackets (`<`, `>`), the script will either throw an "Undefined index" warning or generate broken HTML. Furthermore, echoing variables directly into the `<body>` tag without checking their existence or sanitizing them is a security risk that can lead to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

### Correct Implementation Pattern

To resolve this robustly, you need to combine the DOCTYPE fix with proper PHP output handling. First, ensure `myform.php` starts with the DOCTYPE declaration inside the HTML structure if it is also serving as a page, or better yet, separate concerns by echoing only the necessary data within a valid HTML skeleton.

Here is a corrected version of `myform.php` that handles missing data gracefully and prevents XSS vulnerabilities:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Form Results</title>
</head>
<body>
    <?php
    // Define default values for fields that might be empty
    $name = isset($_POST['name']) ? $_POST['name'] : '';
    $course = isset($_POST['course']) ? $_POST['course'] : '';
    $book = isset($_POST['book']) ? $_POST['book'] : '';
    // Add other variables similarly...

    // Sanitize and escape output to prevent XSS
    echo htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
    ?>
</body>
</html>
```

### Using Modern Frameworks for Scale

For projects where you need to handle more complex routing, validation, or templating without writing raw PHP logic in every view file, consider using a modern framework. Laravel is an excellent choice for building robust web applications that handle form submissions securely out of the box. It abstracts away the `$_POST` superglobals and provides built-in methods to validate input before processing it.

If you are looking to scale beyond simple static forms, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) offer insights into how modern PHP frameworks manage these interactions with greater efficiency and security. By moving from raw `$_POST` access to framework-specific request handling, you eliminate many of the pitfalls associated with manual string concatenation and type checking.

### Final Checklist

To fix your immediate issue:
1.  Add `<!DOCTYPE html>` to the top of both files.
2.  Use `isset()` checks or default values before accessing array keys.
3.  Always wrap user input in `htmlspecialchars()` when echoing it back.

These steps ensure the browser renders the page correctly and that your application remains secure against common web vulnerabilities.
